name: Iris Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Iris, thank you for agreeing to talk. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a restoration firm that repairs old buildings, mostly listed ones, which means the law protects them and you can't just rip things out. This month we're on a Victorian school being turned into flats, so I'm in the workshop repairing sash windows, splicing new oak into rotten frames. Our lead joiner, Mr Okafor, checks every joint I cut, and about half of them he makes me do again. I'm two years in and still slow, but I'm getting cleaner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that a window someone made in 1880 is going to last another hundred years because of something I did. What wears me out is the fine work, my eyes ache by four o'clock, and the cold workshop in winter. I grew up helping in my parents' corner shop and left school early to work there full time, so I came to this late. My fiancé Rohan is an electrician, and we're getting married next September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd be glad. Proper skills take years, and you can't shortcut them with a computer. I'd probably say that to my dad, who's been worried about me for months because of the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can finish learning the trade properly. Mr Okafor says it takes ten years to be a real restoration joiner, and I'd like to get there. Then maybe one day Rohan and I run something small together, him on the wiring and me on the joinery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing exactly what I'm doing. I've got about four months saved, plus the wedding fund, and I'd keep adding to both. I'd keep using AI now and then to look up how old joints were made, that's about all I use it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful. Like being able to breathe out after holding it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you look up with the AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old methods, mostly. Last month I had a window with a joint I'd never seen, and I described it and it told me it was probably a kind of wedged tenon. Mr Okafor said it was right, but he also said I should have asked him first, and he was right too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the wedding planning going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy. Both families want different things, mine want a big celebration with three hundred people, Rohan's want something quieter. In this picture we'd just carry on with the big one, my mum's been saving for it for years.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised and I'm glad, because proper skills take years and can't be shortcut with a computer. I'd say that to my dad, who's been worried because of the news.
S0.think: Privately it means she can finish learning restoration joinery properly over ten years. One day she and her fiancé Rohan might run something small together.
S0.do: Keeps working at the restoration firm and adds to her four months of savings and the wedding fund. Uses AI now and then to look up historic joinery methods.
S0.feel: Calm and grateful, like breathing out after holding it in.
S0.quote: Mr Okafor said it was right, but he also said I should have asked him first, and he was right too.
S0.fieldNote: Iris treats AI as a reference book while respecting her mentor's authority, which she shows in a small, telling story. Family is central: worried parents, a big wedding and a hope of a joint business with her fiancé. She came to the trade late after working in her parents' shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say restoration's different, people want things done by hand on old buildings, and the rules protect that. I'd say firms should keep training young people properly. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be mostly fine for a good while. The conservation officers, the people who check the work on listed buildings, would want proper craft. Maybe the surveying and drawings change, with scanners and so on, but the joinery stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep learning. If the firm brings in a scanner or AI for the surveys, I'd learn it once Mr Okafor's happy with it. And I'd keep saving the same, there's no reason to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little curious about the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rules protect handwork. What if the rules changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in trouble, honestly. But changing them takes years, and people who love old buildings are loud. My church has fought the council over its windows for three years already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rohan, a bit. He does new-build wiring, and that's more standard work, so it might change faster. But he picks things up quicker than me, so I think he'd be all right.

S1.say: I'd say restoration is different because people want handwork on old buildings and the rules protect it. Firms should keep training young people properly.
S1.think: Privately she thinks they'd be fine for a good while because conservation officers want proper craft. Surveying and drawings might change, but the joinery would stay.
S1.do: Keeps working and learning, and learns any new survey scanner or AI tool once her lead joiner approves it. Keeps saving at the same rate without panicking.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little curious about new tools.
S1.quote: My church has fought the council over its windows for three years already.
S1.fieldNote: Iris sees heritage rules and conservation officers as a protective wall around her craft. She would adopt new tools only after her mentor approves. Her worry, mild here, turns towards her fiancé's more standard new-build work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the people who built this should have to answer for it. I'd say families and communities have to look after each other, because you can't count on anyone else. At the temple I'd expect a lot of people asking the same questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried, but maybe not as much as some. Restoration might be one of the last things they automate, because rich people and the heritage rules want human hands. But if a robot can splice oak better than me, which it probably can, then I'm only safe as long as people feel sentimental.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Rohan and I would scale back the wedding, smaller venue, fewer guests, and put the difference into savings. I'd try to get as good as I can, fast, because the best restoration joiners will last longest. And I'd talk to my parents about whether the shop could take one of us on if things go badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but the wedding plans make it harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your families take the smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be upset, she's been saving for years. But she'd understand, she and Dad started the shop with nothing and they're careful with money. Rohan's mum would secretly be pleased, she wanted it small anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're only safe as long as people feel sentimental. Is that enough to plan a life on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. That's the honest answer. But it's what I've got, and I'd rather lean on it than throw away two years of training.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and the people who built it should answer for it. Families and communities have to look after each other, because you can't count on anyone else.
S2.think: Privately she thinks restoration may be among the last things automated because heritage rules and wealthy owners want human hands. But she's only safe as long as people feel sentimental.
S2.do: Scales back the wedding with Rohan and puts the difference into savings. Works to improve quickly as a restoration joiner and asks her parents whether their shop could take one of them on if things go badly.
S2.feel: Anxious but not falling apart, with the wedding plans making it harder.
S2.quote: If a robot can splice oak better than me, which it probably can, then I'm only safe as long as people feel sentimental.
S2.fieldNote: Iris's specialist niche gives her a reason for partial hope even in the fast picture, but she admits it's thin. The wedding is where the change hits first and most visibly. She leans on family and her parents' shop as the fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so people should use it sensibly. I'd say young people should get proper trade training while they can, because real skill still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years makes me feel a bit better. I could get properly good in that time, good enough that a museum or a cathedral wants me, not just any firm. I'd be thirty-two, married, and maybe with the best skills I'll ever have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heritage carpentry qualification Mr Okafor keeps mentioning, starting next year, on day release if the firm allows. I'd keep the wedding as planned but maybe a bit smaller, and keep saving towards six months. Once other restorers start using robots for the rough work, I'd learn to work alongside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I can see a way forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the heritage qualification rather than something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the top of my trade is the last place the robots will reach. Mr Okafor's done work in two cathedrals, people wait a year for him. I'd want to be near that level, not be one of many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still have them, but maybe wait until we see how it's going. My mum would be horrified at that. But I'd want to know Rohan or I had steady work first.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to prepare sensibly. Young people should get proper trade training while they can, because real skill still counts.
S3.think: Privately five years makes her feel better: she could become good enough for museums or cathedrals. At thirty-two she'd be married and at her peak skill.
S3.do: Starts a heritage carpentry qualification next year on day release and keeps the wedding, slightly smaller, while saving towards six months. Learns to work alongside robots once other restorers start using them.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, seeing a way forward.
S3.quote: Because the top of my trade is the last place the robots will reach.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Iris plans to climb to the top of her niche, betting that the most skilled heritage work will last longest. Her mentor's cathedral reputation is her model. She would delay children until work feels steady, knowing her mother would disapprove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people who work hard and plan will be fine. I'd tell my younger cousins to learn a proper trade or a skill that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd get the qualification, get really good, and still have years of work before it lands. At thirty-seven, I'd hope to be a senior joiner, maybe with our own little firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep going and get married next September as planned, the full wedding. Then the heritage qualification over two or three years. Around year five, if robots are on sites, Rohan and I would decide whether to start our own small restoration business while there's still demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only at the back of my mind. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything ten years lets you do that the faster pictures don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have the wedding my mum wants, honestly. And start a family without feeling reckless. In the two-year one everything's about saving; in this one we can live a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd put things off with so much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, because Mr Okafor wouldn't let me. He's sixty-three and he wants to pass it all on before he retires. If anything, he'd push me faster.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people who work hard and plan will be fine. I'd tell my younger cousins to learn a proper trade or a lasting skill.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels manageable: time to qualify, get really good and work for years before it arrives. At thirty-seven she hopes to be a senior joiner, perhaps with her own firm.
S4.do: Marries Rohan next September with the full wedding as planned and takes the heritage qualification over two or three years. Around year five, decides with Rohan whether to start a small restoration business while demand lasts.
S4.feel: Uneasy only at the back of her mind, mostly hopeful.
S4.quote: In the two-year one everything's about saving; in this one we can live a bit.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years restores her family plans: the big wedding and starting a family without feeling reckless. Her mentor's wish to pass on his skills before retiring would keep her from putting things off. A joint restoration business with her husband becomes a real option.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the wedding, the family, the training, everything gets squeezed at once. What would help is firms keeping apprentices on and heritage rules that still ask for real craftspeople, plus family sticking together, which mine would.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum's savings. She's been putting money aside for my wedding since I was ten. Whatever happens with robots, I don't want her to feel that was wasted.

headlineQuote: She's been putting money aside for my wedding since I was ten. Whatever happens with robots, I don't want her to feel that was wasted.
portrait: Iris Gupta is a 27-year-old junior restoration joiner repairing sash windows and oak frames in listed buildings, who came to the trade late after working in her parents' corner shop. She is engaged to Rohan, an electrician, has about four months saved plus a wedding fund, and uses AI now and then to look up old joinery methods. She is calm in the first two pictures, trusting heritage rules to protect handwork. AGI in two years makes her anxious and squeezes the wedding, while five or ten years lead her to aim for the top of her niche, with a cathedral-level mentor as her model.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because the wedding, family plans and training would all be squeezed at once.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping apprentices on, heritage rules that still require real craftspeople, and her family sticking together.
